Newcomer-FAQs & Community-Recommended Resources [SEP] >**Any post which can be answered or addressed by this FAQ is subject to removal and redirection to this thread, at the discretion of the mods.** ¬¬¬¬¬¬¬¬¬¬¬¬¬¬¬¬¬¬¬¬¬¬¬¬¬¬¬¬¬¬¬¬¬¬¬¬¬ **NEW-COMER FAQS** ¬¬¬¬¬¬¬¬¬¬¬¬¬¬¬¬¬¬¬¬¬¬¬¬¬¬¬¬¬¬¬¬¬¬¬¬¬ 1. **Whats the meaning/purpose of life, existence, etc?** | The Existentialist believes that we dont and cant know for sure, because were not able to access absolute knowledge about the nature of our reality. Instead, the fundamentally subjective nature of the way in which we perceive our world means that meaning is created through the exercise of that subjectivityin other words, that we create meaning for ourselves through the use of our Agency. Meaning doesnt exist in the world as an inherent property; instead, its created by us as we assign it to things that we believe are meaningful. 2. **What happens after we die?** | The answer here is, again, that we cant know because were not able to access absolute knowledge about the nature of our reality. We have no reason to trust that anyone can know for suretherefore, we have no reason to trust anyone who tries to tell us that they do. Instead of living as a slave to what *might* come after we die, the Existentialist believes that we can only live according to what we believe that we *can* experience in the nowin other words, in the world which we inhabit while we are alive. 3. **Whats the difference between Nihilism, Absurdism, and Existentialism?** | [Popular consensus]( dictates that Nihilism is: *the rejection of all religious and moral principles, and the belief that life is \[inherently\] meaningless.* Absurdism can be defined as the embracing of this principle of inherent meaninglessness, and thereafter the act of striving to live ones life to its fullest potential in spite of it. Existentialism, meanwhile, is neither the rejection of meaning, nor the embracing of an *inherently* meaningless existenceinstead, its the rejection of this idea of *inherence* itself. The Existentialist does not believe that existence is *inherently* meaningless; instead, he believes that meaning (and therefore also *meaninglessness* itself) is not and cannot be *inherent* to existence& **because meaning is something that we create.** 4. **Do we have Free Will, or do we live in a Deterministic universe?** | The Existentialist believes that we dont and cant know, again because were not able to access absolute knowledge about the nature of our reality. Instead, regardless of the true metaphysical nature of our existenceregardless of whether or not we actually really do have Free Willwe live in a world in which it *appears* obvious to us that we have Agency; that we have the ability to act upon and change the state of our reality. The world which we inhabit *appears* real to usand, until there comes a time when we might discover that its not, there isnt really any good reason for us to treat it as though its not. 5. **What should we do with our Agency?** | The Existentialist believes that this is up to *you*to each individual personto decide. Your choices are yours, and yours alone, and nobody else can really answer this question for you. There is no *should* for you to address with your Agencyonly what you *decide* to do with it. 6. **My life sucks. What do I do?** | Exercise your Agency. Try to figure out how to change your circumstances and situation. *We are abandoned upon the earth*, and you have no reason to believe that anybodys going to come and save you. Therefore, if you want something to change, then *youre* going to have to be the one who goes out and makes it happen. And if it hasnt worked, didnt work, or is still just not working? Go ahead and lie down and give up& or try again, and try harder. Reallyyou can do what you want. Our choices are either determined or they are arbitrary [SEP] I genuinely don't understand libertarianism as a concept. If there is no explanation behind our choices, what does it even mean to say that we are making them? I've read up a bit on agent indeterminism and event indeterminism, but they honestly just seem like nonsense to me. Here's on outline of my though process: 1. For every true fact **X**, there either exists a set of reasons **R** that provides sufficient explanation as to why **X** versus **not X**, or there does not. 2. If **R** exists, then **X** must follow necessarily from **R**, because if **R** could lead to both **X** and **not X**, then **R** does not provide sufficient explanation for **X**. 3. If no **R** exists for some **X**, then that's the definition of arbitrary. There's no reason for **X** to be true, it just happens to be that way. 4. If every single choice or action is either determined or arbitrary, then there is no room left for libertarianism. I think most libertarians would take issue with 3, but I cannot conceive of a fact that could be true without reason or explanation, while also not being arbitrary.

Life is a TV show [SEP] Life is like a tv show. It starts, it gets good. It has downs... but you fall in love with it. Some go on for a long time and some end quickly. But it ends. It has to. If it didn't end then it would get boring. You'd look at the tv show and think "this is just the same stuff but re-written". And that's the thing with life. It's people looking into life and finding a reason to be there. To find excitement and find enjoyment. After a time they accomplish this and can live until they die. And the cycle repeats. Another person watching a new tv show finding a reason to finish it. The meaning of life is nothing but a basic, natural instinct to reproduce. To keep the Species going to "watch more TV shows". So if it's just going to end and the only reason to be here is to keep the Species going then what's the point? There is none. However you can read this is two lights. The side, such as myself, who sees it as a free opportunity to go out and enjoy what you do and to find new and wondrous things to explore. Take every day as if it's the final episode... or... You can look at it as there's no reason to be in this loop, only certain that death is how it ends. That's how I used to be. Thinking that life wasn't anything more than being around and dying. But if you remember the TV shows, they have exciting parts and sad parts throughout them. Your favourite characters die. Some get together with who you "shipped" and some leave and never come back. You get to experience all this and find more and more reasons to stick about. Currently I'm at an impasse with emotion. Confident that I know that life is amazing and terrible because you know that the show has to end, but know that if it didn't you'd get bored. You'd run out of stuff to watch and get excited about. You also know that everyone you love with eventually end too. But remember what I said before? They were practically the same but there was stuff in the middle of the loop and dying. That person's show has gotten to its final episode and the story can't go on any longer. I experience a feeling of no other. I couldn't explain how I felt. You can experience as much as you want but every experience is the same. You stand up in a crowd and do the thing you've always wanted to do. The feelings rush and wash over you. And then it fades. The semantics of the term "free will" are NOT up for debate when discussed in the context of metaphysics and philosophy [SEP] It interests me really, why would we be so split on which definition is best for free will? I'm not saying you're wrong but the way I understand it is that free will should be separated from "will." We all possess a will. Will: We have desires, wants, beliefs, motivations, intuitions, and reasons to do what we do. We possess the ability to choose what we want and act the way we want. It's our volition, it's our will, and the choice is ours as well. The word free is always used to denote the negation or absence of the influence of something. Say, for example, that I buy a book and the shop gives me one more for free. Free of charge, that's what free means in this context. Being released from prison would, for example, mean free of typical prison duties, prison guards, and prison restrictions that can impede a person's actions. Your locus of personal freedom (acting as per your volition) shrinks when your surroundings contain agents who posses "well-being threatening" amounts power of action **and**, more importantly, desires, motivations, and beliefs that conflict with your own. Environments that threaten well-being (like living in a desert or in a low-income household with abusive parents) also produce a similar effect. Free will does not refer to a sort of magical ability that we possess, it merely states that our wills are free off something, and *that* something seems to be the root cause of this whole confusion over the semantics of free will. Now, we can be free of being enslaved by other human beings, free from being threatened by a criminal, free from being forced by a person or something in our environment or an illness inside our bodies to do whatever we want. That's personal liberty and basic/optimum humans rights/living conditions. But when you're talking heavy duty metaphysics, you're talking about the philosophical notion of free will in the context of determinism being the opposing view. Are human thoughts, choices, and actions free of causes that are not initiated or caused by the agent themselves? And the answer is very clear. Either they are not, in which case it would mean that our wills are not free of said causes, or the alternative scenario where we do author the thoughts, desires, and reasons that directly lead to our decisions and actions, but that will make you fall into an infinite regress since at some point across the chain of thoughts and wills, they'd have either spawned randomly out of thin air (or hopefully neurobiology can figure it out) or you must provide newer links to the chain of reason and thoughtÓ_x000F_ which results in an infinite regress. We possess wills but our wills aren't the product of causes initiated/caused by us, the agent. Our wills aren't free of being caused by prior causes that we aren't responsible for. Either that or our wills possess some quasi quantum-mechanical properties and pop up from thin air until they become apparent and intelligible to us.

What Do You Guys Think Of These Arguments For Free-Will?: [SEP] 1. The will is incorporeal. 2. What is incorporeal cannot be moved/changed by a body. 3. The will cannot be influenced by a body, which is to be free. A few things about this argument: to understand it, you need to know a few definitions. I define, "Free," as not being unable to be influenced by something external. I am also using the older sense of, "Body," that is, a three dimensional object. And, "Incorporeal," just means that it is not a body. (Also, to influence is just to move or change). The first premise needs a lot of justification, but that doesn't mean there is none. The senses are limited to knowing things that are here, and now. When you sense something, it has to be in a particular place, and a particular time. Thus, the senses are limited to bodies, because all that is in a place is things with three dimensions. But, on the other hand, the mind, or reason, is not restricted to here and now, but it knows the always, and the everywhere. When I know a Euclid proposition, for example, I don't know this or that triangle, I know what is common to every triangle, that is, I know something that is always true, and true everywhere. But since bodies cannot be everywhere, or always, my knowledge of the everywhere, and the always cannot be a body. And, since my knowledge is in my mind, my mind cannot be a body. And, because the will proceeds from the mind, and the mind is not a body, the will must also not be a body. Phew! That was a lot of philosophically dense text. I think a lot of people will disagree with this, but who knows. And then, the justification for the second premise I think is just rooted in basic physics. An objection that might be thrown in, is that other incorporeal things might be able to influence you, but I can argue against those. The first thing that may be incorporeal, is other people, but the only way people can move or change others is by moving their bodies, to either communicate, or force the other person to do something. But again, bodies cannot effect the will, so this is moot. Then, there may be other incorporeal things, such as angels, or God, but a lot of people don't think those exist, and even if they did, there are arguments for why it cannot be the case that they move us, or why we are still free if they do. Then, there is another thing, someone might ask: "How can something incorporeal, (the will), move something corporeal, (the human body), while something corporeal, (anything bodily), can't move the incorporeal, (the will)?" My answer to that is, the incorporeal is more powerful than the corporeal, and it is evident that what is more powerful can move what is less powerful, while the less powerful cannot move the more powerful. Such as the wind can move a branch, but a branch cannot move the wind. Anyway, what do you guys think?

A second or a lifetime? Does it matter? Does it all matter? [SEP] When you're younger the world is so simple. You view life upwards as so far away. You're immortal. But when I hit 30 (currently 36 at the time of writing this) I had a brutal existential crisis, which still effects me most days. For context, I'm an atheist. I have no problem with people following a religion, but looking at the world, I just can't believe there is a magic afterlife. I'm jealous of people with that comfort. Side note, I used to work in a Cathedral and would often walk through the Nave thinking "God, if you're there, in a super holy place, give me a sign" but I never felt anything. However our Dean was once a sound engineer and heard God tell her to become a priest... One day, I was laying in bed at night in the dark and thinking about death, which I guess was triggered by the shock of turning 30. For one split second I imagined what it would be like not to exist after death. It scared the shit out of me and for the next year or two I had a super bad existential crisis. --------------------------- It made me seriously ponder a question: "is there a difference between living one second or 100 years?" --------------------------- This feeling, still hits me often, usually at night and it is like having my guts sucked out of me with a cold wave. I guess I'm describing that cold wave you get when you remember something terrible. I thought I had turned a corner from it but it's always in the back of my mind when I see someone die on a film or a series on TV. I feel sad for the passing of life. Its actually been one of the driving forces behind going vegan (I was already veggie), as I can't stand living creatures losing their right to exist for me to eat. I've got a good life, love my work, got great friends, travel the world and importantly I have a loving partner and a wonderful relationship. I guess this is something I'll never get over. But if anyone has had a similar experience and come through it, I'd love to know your thoughts. Questions for the group: - if it all goes black and we stop existing, is there any point? My drive is to live every possible second and stay alive, but if you just die, with nothing afterwards isn't that the most terrifying thought? - those who theorise that this is a simulation, do you hope they programmed an afterlife? Haha - those of you who are religious: 1. How would you feel if you spent your life worshipping a god and it wasn't true? 2. I guess if you're wrong, you'll never know, because your be dead, but is it a life wasted? What about priests? I'm sure I'm missing thoughts, ideas and contemplations. It's hard to put it down on paper. But it's am and I can't sleep because I'm shit scared of one day passing away. God I hope I'm wrong and there is an afterlife!
